article_blocks.text: Strain Type: Autoflowering hybrid
Genetics: Power Plant × Ruderalis Indica
Breeder: Dutch Passion
THC Content: 19%
CBD Content: N/A
Terpene Profile: N/A
Primary Flavors: Sweet herbs, earth, spice, subtle citrus
Flowering Time (Indoor): 8–10 weeks from seed to harvest
Outdoor Harvest Time: 8-10 weeks
Indoor Yield: 25–30 grams per plant
Outdoor Yield: 25–30 grams per plant
Grow Difficulty: Easy

Taiga belongs to the first generation of Dutch Passion autoflowers, when automatic flowering was still considered an unusual cannabis trait rather than a mainstream category. Instead of designing a plant around modern Cookies, candy, or dessert genetics, Dutch Passion reached into one of its most established sativa-dominant breeding lines: Power Plant. An exceptionally early-flowering Power Plant female was selected and crossed with a compact autoflowering Ruderalis/Indica, allowing the breeder to retain much of Power Plant’s recognizable flower character while forcing the resulting marijuana to mature according to age rather than a seasonal light change. The original plant could move from seed to finished flower in roughly eight to ten weeks while remaining only about 50–60 centimeters tall—an extraordinary level of compactness for its era. Historical Dutch Passion descriptions emphasized large, tight buds for such a small plant, straightforward feeding requirements, and a flavor strongly reminiscent of Power Plant.

What makes the cultivar worth remembering today is not that it can outperform the newest autoflowers. Modern automatic genetics have become considerably larger, stronger, and more productive. Taiga matters because it represents part of the transition that made those later plants possible. Dutch Passion continued refining its autoflower program after the original release, eventually replacing Taiga with Taiga #2 as part of a 2013 upgrade intended to improve strength, yield, and consistency. The breeder’s own announcement described that second version as an evolution of the successful original rather than an unrelated strain.
Genetics and Lineage

The original pedigree begins with Power Plant, one of Dutch Passion’s long-running sativa-dominant varieties , crossed with a selected autoflowering Ruderalis/Indica. Historical breeder material explains that Dutch Passion searched its Power Plant gene pool for an unusually early-flowering female, induced that female to produce feminized pollen, and used the pollen on the selected automatic female. This is more specific than simply describing Taiga as “Power Plant × Ruderalis,” because the automatic parent also carried indica influence and the Power Plant parent was chosen for unusually early maturation.

Power Plant gives the strain most of its recognizable recreational cannabis identity. Dutch Passion developed that parent from South African genetics, and it became known for vigorous growth, substantial flower production, a strong cerebral character, and an earthy-spicy aromatic profile. Taiga was intended to bring those qualities into a dramatically smaller and quicker format. The Ruderalis/Indica side supplied the automatic flowering mechanism, short stature, and rapid lifecycle, traits that allowed plants to flower without waiting for decreasing daylight hours or an indoor switch to 12/12 lighting.

This combination also explains why the original Taiga should not be confused with Taiga #2. Dutch Passion announced in late 2012 that Taiga, Tundra, and PolarLight were being upgraded after several more years of autoflower breeding. The improved Taiga #2 still relied on Power Plant genetics but was bred for greater consistency, potency, and yield. Dutch Passion’s later description placed Taiga #2 closer to 100 centimeters with reports of 100 grams or more per plant, dramatically exceeding the 50–60 centimeter stature and roughly 25–30 gram historical yield of the original.
Effects and Experience

Taiga’s effect reflects an early attempt to preserve the personality of a conventional photoperiod strain inside an autoflowering framework. Power Plant contributes a mentally active element that can make the opening portion feel brighter and more engaging than the plant’s squat appearance suggests. Mood may rise, conversation can become easier, and music or visual entertainment may feel more involving. Rather than beginning as an overwhelmingly heavy indica, the experience can retain a recognizable cerebral edge.

Physical relaxation becomes more noticeable after that initial lift. The Ruderalis/Indica contribution and the hybridized structure of the plant create a steadier body sensation beneath the mental effects, making the overall experience more balanced than a pure sativa. Dutch Passion’s later Taiga #2 retained this same general reputation, with the breeder describing a powerful, long-lasting effect that could support creativity before settling into a stronger body stone. A Dutch Passion grow report similarly described Taiga #2 as producing a pleasant high followed by a comfortable physical effect, suggesting that the basic experiential character survived the later breeding work.

A reliable THC figure for the original release was never published by Dutch Passion, so modern percentage claims should be treated cautiously. Some later retailers assign numerical potency ranges, but those numbers are not equivalent to breeder-verified laboratory results from the original genetic release. Consumers should therefore judge strength from the actual product rather than assuming a fixed THC percentage. Even moderately potent marijuana can impair short-term memory, judgment, coordination, and reaction time, and excessive amounts may produce anxiety, dizziness, or unwanted sedation.
Medical Benefits

No clinical research has evaluated Taiga itself as a treatment for a medical condition. Early autoflower strains were often marketed toward self-sufficient recreational and medical growers because their small size and rapid lifecycle made home production more accessible, but that horticultural usefulness does not establish strain-specific therapeutic effects.

Research involving cannabis more broadly suggests modest benefits for some forms of chronic pain , while cannabinoid medicines have established uses in a limited number of conditions. NCCIH notes that research on sleep, anxiety, and many other commonly discussed applications remains less certain, and that benefits seen with standardized cannabinoid products cannot automatically be transferred to a particular marijuana flower strain.

For someone using cannabis medically, the lack of a standardized cannabinoid profile is particularly important. Two surviving Taiga plants could differ meaningfully in THC, CBD, and terpene expression, especially given the age and rarity of the original genetics. THC may also produce dizziness, sleepiness, anxiety, cognitive impairment, or drug interactions in some people. Medical consumers should therefore rely on current laboratory testing and appropriate professional guidance rather than historical strain descriptions.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

Power Plant provides the clearest reference point for Taiga’s aroma. Historical Dutch Passion descriptions explicitly state that the smell and flavor strongly resemble the photoperiod parent, giving the flower a more traditional cannabis profile than the dessert-like autoflowers developed later. Sweet herbs and earth form much of the base, accompanied by spicy, woody, and lightly citrus qualities.

The smell can become considerably stronger as the compact flowers mature. Rather than producing an intensely fruity or candy-like bouquet, well-cured flower leans toward pungent herbaceous sweetness with dry spice underneath. That profile is especially characteristic of cannabis genetics developed before modern fruit-candy breeding became dominant. On the palate, mild sweetness may appear first, followed by earthy herbs and pepper-like spice through the finish.

No credible breeder-issued terpene analysis exists for the original cultivar. It would therefore be misleading to state that myrcene, limonene, caryophyllene, or another terpene dominates at a particular percentage. Historical aroma descriptions provide firmer evidence than retrospective terpene guesses. Storage remains important as well; warm conditions and repeated air exposure can dull the lighter sweet and citrus aspects, leaving older flower tasting considerably more earthy.
Growing Information

Taiga was designed around simplicity. Dutch Passion described it as an easy plant that did not require a specialized feeding schedule, an important advantage during a period when many growers were unfamiliar with autoflowering cannabis. The entire lifecycle ran approximately eight to ten weeks from seed to harvest, eliminating the conventional division between a long vegetative period and photoperiod-triggered flowering.

Typical height was only 50–60 centimeters. Plants remained small and relatively bushy without producing excessive side branching, concentrating much of their production into compact central flowers. Historical breeder material listed approximately 25–30 grams per plant—modest by current autoflower standards but respectable considering the plant’s tiny frame. Dutch Passion also stated that containers of roughly 1.5–2 liters could support a satisfactory crop, another indication of how compact the root system and overall plant were intended to remain.

Outdoors, harvest timing depends on germination date rather than autumn photoperiod. A plant started in late spring can finish during summer, allowing multiple seasonal runs in favorable climates. Dutch Passion specifically emphasized full sun for the best outdoor quality and production. Because autoflowers have little time to recover from major early stress, steady conditions during the first few weeks are disproportionately important. Poor root development, excessive feeding, overwatering, or severe transplant shock can permanently reduce final plant size.

Indoor cultivation follows the same principle. Because the plant flowers automatically, delaying growth through severe training or recovery periods offers little advantage. Gentle canopy management and stable environmental conditions are generally more appropriate than aggressive pruning. Air movement around the compact central flower becomes important as maturity approaches because dense buds can retain moisture even on an otherwise small plant.

The original cultivar’s limited yield eventually became one reason for further breeding. Dutch Passion spent several years improving its AutoFem program and publicly announced a replacement in the form of Taiga #2. The upgraded plant retained Power Plant-derived genetics but offered substantially more resin, stronger effects, greater uniformity, a roughly ten-week lifecycle, and far higher production. Dutch Passion now lists Taiga #2 itself as discontinued, with Auto Power Plant among the recommended modern alternatives.
FAQ
What strain is Taiga?

Taiga is an early Dutch Passion autoflower bred from an unusually early-flowering Power Plant female crossed with an autoflowering Ruderalis/Indica. It was designed to preserve Power Plant-like cannabis quality in a very short automatic plant.
Who bred the Taiga strain?

Dutch Passion created the original Taiga AutoFem. The breeder was one of the early commercial seed companies to invest heavily in feminized autoflower genetics and later upgraded Taiga into Taiga #2 as the technology improved.
Is Taiga the same as Taiga #2?

No. Taiga #2 is an improved later version. Dutch Passion announced the upgrade for 2013, specifically citing improvements in consistency, strength, and yield. The original Taiga typically remained around 50–60 cm and produced roughly 25–30 grams per plant, while Taiga #2 could stay under one meter yet exceed 100 grams per plant in successful grows.
How long does Taiga take from seed to harvest?

The original breeder description gives approximately eight to ten weeks from germination to harvest. Because the cultivar flowers automatically, there is no need to change the light cycle to trigger flowering.
What does Taiga taste like?

The original strain was described as clearly resembling Power Plant in both smell and flavor. Expect a traditional profile of sweet herbs, earth, spice, woody cannabis notes, and mild citrus rather than modern dessert or candy flavors.
Final Thoughts on Taiga

Taiga is far easier to appreciate when viewed as a piece of autoflower breeding history rather than compared directly with current genetics. A plant that stayed 50–60 centimeters tall and yielded roughly an ounce might appear unimpressive beside modern autos capable of producing several times that amount, but those later developments depended on breeders proving that automatic flowering could coexist with recognizable high-quality marijuana genetics.

Dutch Passion used an unusually early Power Plant female and an autoflowering Ruderalis/Indica to pursue exactly that goal. The result carried Power Plant-inspired aroma and cerebral character into a plant that could complete its entire life in roughly eight to ten weeks, needed little root space, and did not require a flowering light-cycle change. The original breeder also emphasized simplicity: no specialized feeding program, compact flowers, and outdoor harvest determined by planting date rather than autumn daylight.

Its limitations became part of its legacy. Dutch Passion continued refining autoflower genetics until it felt capable of improving the original significantly, announcing Taiga #2 alongside upgraded versions of several other early AutoFem marijuana strains . The new generation offered better consistency, strength, resin, and yield while retaining the Power Plant foundation. Dutch Passion’s 2012 announcement makes that breeding progression unusually clear and establishes the original Taiga as a genuine predecessor to the more sophisticated autoflowering marijuana that followed.

For cannabis historians, collectors, and growers interested in the development of automatic genetics, that may be Taiga’s greatest significance. It was never designed to be enormous. It was designed to make a very small plant finish rapidly while still tasting and feeling like recognizable Dutch Passion weed. In that context, Taiga accomplished exactly what it was bred to do and helped establish the foundation for the much larger, stronger, and more productive autoflowers that dominate the category today.
